opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a ladder with a few distinct rungs, and each one changes what we're really asking the model to do.

The first rung is a single agent doing a single task well: you give it a goal, it plans, calls tools, writes code, browses, checks its own work, and comes back with a result. What matters most here is long-horizon reliability. Can it stay on track for hundreds of steps without drifting, and can it recover when something goes wrong? A lot of our recent work has been about that: training models to think and act over long sequences, not just answer in one shot.

The second rung is when the agent stops being a tool you supervise step by step and becomes something closer to a colleague. You hand it an ambiguous objective, and it decides how to break it down, what information it lacks, and when to come back and ask. That needs judgment, not just capability, and judgment is much harder to measure with benchmarks.

The third rung is organization-level capability. That's where many agents, possibly with different specializations, coordinate the way a team or a company does. Some of them generate ideas, some execute, some review, some allocate resources. Once you get there, the bottleneck isn't any single model's intelligence. It's communication, division of labor, shared memory, and how you resolve conflicts and keep everyone aligned to the same goal. Those are the same problems human organizations have always had, just at a different speed and scale.

What excites me is that when you scale up the number of agents and how long they run, you may get something that compounds, the way a good organization is more than the sum of its people. A single person, however brilliant, can't build a modern chip or a large model alone. Civilization-level progress comes from organizations. If AI can reach that level, so that one person, or even one model, can effectively direct a whole organization of agents, then the leverage changes fundamentally.

But I want to be honest that we're still early. Today the single-agent rung isn't fully solved: error accumulation over long tasks is real, and evaluation is hard. My view is that organization-level capability won't come mainly from clever orchestration frameworks on top of weak models. It will come from making the base models much stronger at long-horizon reasoning and at collaborating, ideally learned end to end through training rather than hand-designed. Then the organizational structure can be something the system partly discovers for itself.

So the progression, for me, is from intelligence as answering, to intelligence as doing, to intelligence as organizing. Each step needs a new kind of scaling, and I think that's where a lot of the next few years' breakthroughs will come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression as a ladder with distinct rungs, but does not say that the progression may be nonlinear.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful way to frame it is that an agent today is roughly at the level of an individual contributor. You give it a task, it reasons, it uses tools, it comes back with a result. That's a big step from a chatbot, but it's still fundamentally one unit of work at a time.

The next step is not just making that single agent smarter. It's about what happens when you have many agents, each with different roles, working toward a shared goal over a long time horizon. That's where organization-level capability starts to emerge. An organization isn't just a collection of smart people. It's the division of labor, the communication protocols, the ability to decompose a large problem, run things in parallel, check each other's work, and recover from mistakes without one error collapsing the whole system.

So when I think about the progression, I see a few layers that have to be solved. The first is long-horizon reliability. A single agent that is right ninety percent of the time becomes almost useless when you chain fifty steps together. We need agents that can maintain context, verify their own outputs, and know when to stop and ask. The second is coordination. How does one agent hand off to another? How do they share state? How do you avoid the equivalent of ten people editing the same document with no version control? The third, and I think the hardest, is judgment about goals. An organization doesn't just execute, it decides what's worth doing. That requires models that understand priorities, tradeoffs, and the intent behind an instruction rather than just the literal instruction.

What makes me optimistic is that a lot of this is actually a scaling problem again, just along a different axis. We scaled parameters, then we scaled data, then we scaled inference-time compute. The next axis is scaling the number of agents and the length of time they can operate coherently. Reinforcement learning is central here, because you can train agents not just on individual task completion but on how well the whole system performs when they work together.

If I had to guess at the shape of the curve, I'd say in the near term we'll see small teams of agents that can own a well-scoped project end to end, something like a feature in a codebase or a research report. Over the longer term, you get to something that looks like a company, where you set a direction and the system figures out the org chart itself. That's when AI stops being a productivity tool and becomes a genuinely new kind of economic actor.

r001.rationale: The response describes stages and a possible growth curve, but it does not state that the progression may be nonlinear.

astra-6.text:
I think the key transition is from an agent that can complete a task to a system that can take responsibility for an outcome. Those are quite different things. A task usually comes with a defined objective. At the organization level, you have to decide what the tasks should be, how to divide them, and how to tell whether the overall effort is working.

So having many agents is only part of it. You also need shared context, coordination, and ways to resolve mistakes or conflicting judgments. If each agent performs well locally but they’re working toward different assumptions, the organization can still fail.

The other important piece is learning over time. When one project succeeds or fails, can the system preserve that experience and improve the next project? That’s what makes the capability durable. I’d expect the progression to happen first in bounded workflows, where outcomes are easy to verify, and then expand as these systems become better at coordinating and correcting themselves. Humans still need to set the goals and decide which responsibilities to delegate.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression from bounded workflows to broader capability, but does not state that this progression is not necessarily linear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key transition is from an agent that can complete a task to a system that can take responsibility for an outcome. An individual agent might write code, analyze information, or produce a report. But an organization has to decide what matters, divide the work, coordinate dependencies, evaluate results, and learn from mistakes.

So putting many agents together doesn’t automatically give you an organization. You need shared context, clear responsibilities, and mechanisms for resolving disagreements and checking quality. Otherwise, adding agents can just create more coordination overhead.

I would expect this to develop gradually. First, agents help people with individual tasks. Then they take ownership of longer workflows, with people supervising important decisions. Eventually, systems may coordinate multiple workflows around a broader objective. The meaningful measure is how reliably they achieve that objective, how much human intervention they need, and whether they improve over time.

That also changes the human role. People spend less time specifying every step and more time defining goals, constraints, and what good results look like. I think that is where organization-level capability starts to become interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a gradual sequence from individual tasks to longer workflows and then multiple workflows, but does not say the progression may be nonlinear.
